deep.reconstruction:
This page continues Thesis III of the Latin 'Theses' that Riemann drafted for the public defence of his 1851 Göttingen dissertation, 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse'. The previous page sets up Thesis III, on how a function of a complex variable is determined. It says the usual methods all start from an analytic expression, by means of which, for any ('quovis', split across the page break) given value of the argument, the value of the function is given. This page continues as follows.

Translation: "...for any determined value of the argument the value of the function is given. We, however, have shown that if, in an arbitrarily small region, the values of the function are given for the values of the argument, the values of the function for the remaining values already follow from them. We have also specified the amount of mutually independent conditions that is necessary to determine the function. Therefore, in the usual definition of determined functions of a complex variable, superfluous marks seem to us to be present."

The right-hand fragment ('...um complexae quantitatis variabilis determinatarum') is an insertion. It replaces the struck words 'functionis determinatae', so that the phrase reads 'In vulgari igitur functionum complexae quantitatis variabilis determinatarum definitione...'.

Modern content. There is no computation on the page. Two claims are made.

(a) Identity theorem / uniqueness of analytic continuation. If w = f(z) satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations (Riemann's own definition, from art. 1 of the dissertation) on a connected surface T, then f is determined by its values on any small open subset. Equivalently: f, g analytic on connected T and f = g on an open set (or on a curve segment) implies f = g on T.

(b) Counting of independent data, from arts. 18–20 of the dissertation. A function is determined, up to constants, by independent boundary data. For example, it is fixed by the real part u on the boundary, or by u along the boundary together with the periodicity and singularity conditions; this is done via the Dirichlet principle. It is not fixed by both u and v freely, since those data are not independent.

The polemical point: defining a function by an explicit analytic expression valid everywhere includes redundant information ('notae superfluae'). Riemann's approach characterises the function intrinsically by the differential equation together with a minimal set of determining conditions.
errors: No mathematical errors. The claims are stated informally. The identity theorem requires connectedness of the domain (Riemann's surfaces are assumed connected), which is implicit here.

In the dissertation, the 'amplitudo conditionum' (amount of determining data) rests on the Dirichlet principle. Weierstrass (1870) later showed this was not rigorously justified; Hilbert repaired it around 1900.

results.what: A complex-analytic function on a connected domain is determined everywhere by its values in an arbitrarily small region
results.modern_name: Identity theorem / uniqueness of analytic continuation
results.usually_credited_to: Implicit in Cauchy and Riemann; formalised by Weierstrass (analytic continuation via power series, 1840s–1870s)

results.what: Specification of the amount of independent conditions (boundary values of the real part, discontinuities) needed to determine a function
results.modern_name: Dirichlet problem / Dirichlet principle; Riemann's determination of analytic functions by boundary and singularity data
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (1851 dissertation), building on Dirichlet, Gauss, Green and Thomson

results.what: Polemical thesis: the usual definition of a function by an analytic expression contains superfluous determinations
results.modern_name: Riemann's conceptual (Cauchy–Riemann / boundary-data) definition versus the expression-based (Euler–Lagrange) notion of function

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of the defence theses attached to Riemann's own 1851 dissertation. It restates, in Latin, results already in the published dissertation: the identity theorem and determination of functions via the Dirichlet principle. It is of minor historical interest as a polemical framing against Cauchy, but contains nothing new mathematically.
